pages.text: Red Dwarf is the Jupiter Mining Corporation ship at the centre of the comedy. Its surviving company includes Lister, Rimmer, Cat, Holly and, later, Kryten.
The setting is roughly three million years after the disaster. Blue Midget and Starbug are its shuttlecraft. Try asking about a crew member or one of the ships.
Dave Lister survives the radiation disaster because he is in stasis. Holly wakes him roughly three million years later. His former bunkmate Rimmer returns as a hologram.
Lister was found as a baby beneath a pool table in Liverpool. His later adventures include finding the lost Red Dwarf and learning that time travel makes him his own father.
Craig Charles plays Dave Lister.
Arnold Rimmer is Lister's officious bunkmate, brought back as a hologram after the radiation disaster.
In Series VII he leaves to take up the mantle of Ace Rimmer. Series VIII instead includes a resurrected, pre-accident Rimmer.
Chris Barrie plays Arnold Rimmer.
Cat belongs to a humanoid species descended from Lister's pregnant cat, Frankenstein. The species evolved aboard Red Dwarf over three million years.
He has an enormous interest in clothes and very little interest in work. The official database gives him no personal name beyond Cat.
Danny John-Jules plays Cat.
In Red Dwarf, Holly is the ship's computer. Her original IQ is stated as 6000, but prolonged isolation causes computer senility. That fictional IQ is not a measurement of this Pi.
Holly invents the Holly Hop Drive and falls for Hilly, a counterpart from another universe. Adopting Hilly's face explains the in-story change of appearance.
Norman Lovett and Hattie Hayridge play Holly in the television series.
Kryten 2X4B-523P is a Series 4000 mechanoid and a member of the Red Dwarf crew. Ask about the Kryten episode for his first television appearance.
Unlike a human crewmate, Kryten is an artificial life-form. His records are among the sources used by the fictional Space Corps Database.
David Ross plays Kryten in Series II. Robert Llewellyn takes over when Kryten becomes a regular in Series III.
Kristine Kochanski is Lister's lost love. A counterpart from another universe joins the travelling crew during Series VII.
Kochanski's arrival changes the crew dynamic, especially Kryten's relationship with Lister.
Clare Grogan plays the earlier Kochanski; Chloe Annett plays the parallel-universe version introduced in Ouroboros.
Ace Rimmer is a brave, popular test pilot from a parallel universe. Dimension Jump brings him face to face with Arnold Rimmer.
Dimension Jump is Series IV, episode 5, first broadcast on 14 March 1991. The contrast between the two Rimmers drives the story.
Chris Barrie plays Ace as well as Arnold Rimmer.
Hilly is Holly's counterpart in Parallel Universe, Series II, episode 6. Hattie Hayridge plays her.
The episode uses Holly's hop drive to reach a universe of counterparts, including female versions of Lister and Rimmer.
Hattie Hayridge plays Hilly.
Frankenstein is the pregnant cat Lister smuggles aboard Red Dwarf. Her descendants eventually evolve into the humanoid cat species.
She survives in the cargo hold. Cat religion later treats her as its holy mother.
Cloister is the cat religion's distorted memory of Lister. Its promised destination, Fuchal, grows out of his dream of a diner in Fiji.
The cats divide over whether diner hats should be red or blue, although Lister intended green. Their arks leave Red Dwarf seeking Fuchal.
Duane Dibbley is Cat's uncool alter ego, introduced in Back to Reality.
The character appears in Series V's finale, which questions the crew's identities.
The Aigburth Arms is the Liverpool pub where baby Lister was found beneath a pool table. Ouroboros confirms the pub's identity.
Baby Lister in Ouroboros is played by Alexander John-Jules, Danny John-Jules' nephew.
Starbug is a JMC shuttle used by the crew. It is equipped for difficult terrain and underwater salvage, although its crash record leaves room for improvement.
Its arrangements include a cockpit, sleeping quarters, galley and medical facilities. Ore sample pods have also served as improvised escape pods.
Blue Midget is another JMC craft used for journeys between a ship and a planetary surface.
Its walker legs help it cross rough terrain. The official database also celebrates its ability to dance, which is an unusual entry on a spacecraft specification.
Skutters are Red Dwarf's maintenance robots. Bob and Madge are two named examples.
They enjoy John Wayne films and western games. Their willingness to insult Rimmer suggests maintenance is not their only talent.
Talkie Toaster is an artificial intelligence devoted to toast with exhausting enthusiasm. Lister eventually attacks it with a heavy hammer.
It was made by Crapola Inc. The joke is a machine whose entire conversation keeps returning to its one domestic purpose.
John Lenahan voices the early Toaster. David Ross voices it in White Hole and later Mechocracy.
Simulants are dangerous artificial beings with biomechanical elements. They were built for a war that never happened and seek opponents across space.
Some treat hunting humans as sport. One pair even upgrades Starbug before pursuing the crew, making the chase more interesting for themselves.
The Holly Hop Drive is Holly's invention for travelling beyond the crew's own universe. Its adventure brings Holly into contact with Hilly.
This is fictional Red Dwarf technology. This OS has no propulsion system, dimension drive, or control over a real spacecraft.
In White Hole, intelligence compression restores Holly's genius but leaves her with less than four minutes of operating life.
The story trades intelligence against remaining lifespan. It is a comedy premise, not how this Pi's model or processor works.
Rimmer is an electronic reconstruction of a dead crewmate. The fictional Space Corps Database refers to his light-bee as a source of records.
Red Dwarf treats holographic people as personalities, not merely recordings to watch. Rimmer continues to argue and interact with the others.
The End opens Series I. A radiation accident kills the mining ship's crew while Lister survives in stasis. He awakens three million years later.
First broadcast: 15 February 1988 on BBC2. Rob Grant and Doug Naylor wrote it; Ed Bye directed it.
Future Echoes is Series I, episode 2. When the ship exceeds light speed, the crew see events from their future, including an apparent fatal explosion.
First broadcast: 22 February 1988. The official guide notes that the TV victim is Lister's son Bexley, while the novel changes that family relationship.
Kryten, Series II episode 1, introduces the android on the Nova 5. The rescue party discovers that the women he serves are long dead.
First broadcast: 6 September 1988. David Ross plays Kryten, who was initially intended as a one-off character.
Better Than Life is Series II, episode 2. A game offers wish fulfilment, but Rimmer's mind makes enjoying it rather less straightforward.
First broadcast: 13 September 1988. This card describes the television episode; the novel with the same title is a separate work.
Queeg is Series II, episode 5. A supposed backup computer takes over from Holly and imposes a punishing work-and-fitness routine.
First broadcast: 4 October 1988. Charles Augins plays Queeg; Norman Lovett plays Holly.
Charles Augins plays Queeg.
Parallel Universe closes Series II. Holly's hop drive takes the crew to a world with female Lister and Rimmer, Hilly, and a Dog counterpart to Cat.
First broadcast: 11 October 1988. Hattie Hayridge appears as Hilly. The episode also contains the Tongue Tied musical sequence.
Polymorph is Series III, episode 3. A shape-changing genetic creature gets aboard Red Dwarf and terrorises the crew.
First broadcast: 28 November 1989. The remastered edition adds a caption addressing the second polymorph, a detail left unresolved in the original.
White Hole is Series IV, episode 4. Holly regains her genius, powers down the ship, and leaves the others facing a dangerous white hole.
First broadcast: 7 March 1991. Its plot draws on material first used in the Better Than Life novel.
Dimension Jump is Series IV, episode 5. Ace Rimmer crosses from another universe and meets his very different counterpart.
First broadcast: 14 March 1991. Ace is a test pilot; his competence and popularity make Arnold's insecurities particularly visible.
Quarantine is Series V, episode 4. After a visit to a viral research centre, Rimmer orders the other crew into twelve weeks of isolation.
First broadcast: 12 March 1992. Maggie Steed plays Dr Hildegarde Lanstrom. Mr Flibble also appears in this episode.
Mr Flibble is the penguin hand puppet associated with Rimmer in Quarantine. It became one of the show's memorable visual jokes.
Howard Burden assembled the puppet as a temporary solution, but the production kept it rather than replacing it.
Back to Reality closes Series V. The crew investigates a submerged spacecraft whose occupants died, then faces a giant sea creature and a crisis of identity.
First broadcast: 26 March 1992. Timothy Spall plays Andy. The episode's arcade set reuses the Enlightenment set from Holoship.
Legion is Series VI, episode 2. With supplies running low, the crew is drawn to an apparently deserted space station.
First broadcast: 14 October 1993. Nigel Williams plays Legion. Lister's appendix operation is a noted continuity problem because an earlier episode mentions its removal.
Nigel Williams plays Legion.
Gunmen of the Apocalypse is Series VI, episode 3. The crew enters Kryten's electronic mind to fight a computer virus represented as western gunslingers.
First broadcast: 28 October 1993. The episode won the International Emmy for Popular Arts in 1994; its western scenes were filmed at Laredo in Kent.
Ouroboros is Series VII, episode 3. A meeting between realities brings an alternate Kochanski aboard, making Kryten anxious about losing Lister's attention.
First broadcast: 31 January 1997. This is Chloe Annett's first appearance as Kochanski.
The Promised Land is a feature-length Red Dwarf special first broadcast on 9 April 2020. It returns to the civilisation descended from Lister's cat.
Doug Naylor wrote and directed it. Norman Lovett appears as Holly; Ray Fearon plays Rodon.
The novels include Infinity Welcomes Careful Drivers and Better Than Life, followed by Doug Naylor's Last Human and Rob Grant's Backwards.
The books expand and reinterpret television ideas. Their events should not automatically be treated as identical to TV continuity.
The official FAQ does not settle exactly which Rimmer appears after Series VIII or how he became a hologram again. A confident invented explanation would be misleading.
Back to Earth takes place before the real Series X. Its reference to a series ten belongs to the story's hallucination, not the actual later production.
The official Red Dwarf FAQ describes the show as a universe without aliens. Strange beings should not automatically be described as extraterrestrial civilisations.
The FAQ also warns that a background TARDIS model is a production in-joke, not proof of an official Doctor Who crossover.
Smeg is a fictional swear word created for Red Dwarf by Rob Grant and Doug Naylor.
Its resemblance to the name of the Italian appliance company is coincidental, according to the official FAQ.
The guide lists I-II in 1988, III in 1989, IV in 1991, V in 1992, VI in 1993, VII in 1997, and VIII in 1999.
It then lists Back to Earth (2009), X (2012), XI (2016), XII (2017), and The Promised Land (2020). This pack is a curated historical reference, not a live news feed.
